title: Quantification of astrocytic synaptic pruning in mouse hippocampal slices in response to ex vivo Aβ treatment via colocalization analysis with C1q
protocol: Prepare the surgery site with surgical scissors.
Use standard pattern forceps with curved and serrated tips.
Place fresh blades nearby.
Have a spatula ready.
Decapitate the mouse using a guillotine.
Place the mouse brain inside the preparation ringer solution immediately after decapitation.
Ensure the preparation ringer solution is constantly oxygenated with carbogen.
Keep the beaker with the preparation ringer solution in a box full of ice to maintain its slushy state.
Anesthetize the mouse by placing it in an isoflurane chamber with 5% isoflurane concentration and at a flow rate of 2 L/min.
Wait until the animal is unresponsive.
Check for loss of righting reflex.
Pinch the tail to confirm lack of response.
Transfer the decapitated head quickly to a petri dish containing oxygenated preparation ringer solution.
Cut open the scalp through the midline along the sagittal suture with surgical scissors.
Make lateral cuts on both sides of the skull and remove the top of the skull carefully.
Gently lift out the brain from the caudal side using a spatula.
Transfer the brain quickly to iced-cooled preparation ringer solution in a beaker.
Discard mouse body and head properly.
Disinfect and clean the guillotine, anesthetizing chamber, and workspace.
Bring the brain to the microtome setup.
Section the brain in the sagittal plane into 350 μm thick slices for incubation and treatment.
Cut off the cerebellum from the brain using a razor.
Separate the two hemispheres with a sharp razor blade.
Put two streaks of tissue adhesive on the microtome cutting plate.
Dry both hemispheres by transferring them to filter paper for 2-3 seconds.
Transfer the dried brain hemispheres to the tissue adhesive on the microtome plate and secure it in the holder.
Lock the microtome plate securely.
Insert a razor blade inside the microtome.
Set the cutting window from starting to final position.
Adjust the thickness setting to 350 μm.
Trim the hemispheres until anterior hippocampus appears.
Start collecting slices, dividing them into control and treatment beakers.
Cut brain slices carefully using a pipette and transfer them to oxygenated mess ringer-filled beakers in the water bath.
Pay attention to bubbles in nets holding the slices.
Ensure brain slices do not overlap on each other.
Trim sagittal section of the brain, keeping hippocampus and cortex intact if overcrowding occurs.
Place beakers containing slices in water bath at 35°C for about 30 min.
Remove beakers from water bath and incubate at RT (21°C to 24°C) for 1 h.
Pipette out 35 μL of Aβ42 into aCSF solution in the treatment beaker to obtain 50 nM concentration of Aβ42.
Incubate slices with Aβ42 for 90 min at RT (21°C to 24°C) under continuous oxygenation.
Leave control slices in aCSF with continuous oxygenation for 90 min at RT (21°C to 24°C).
Thaw Aβ42 stock solution at RT (21°C to 24°C) twenty min prior to incubation and then place it back in the −20°C freezer.
Place the slices in 30% sucrose solution for cryoprotection.
Divide the slices into a 6-well plate and pour in adequate amount of 4% PFA to cover the slices.
Incubate the slices overnight (16–20 h) on a 3D shaker at 4°C in 4% PFA solution.
Wash the slices three times with 1× PBS for 10 min each.
Add 2 ml of 30% sucrose solution into each well and incubate for 2 days on 3D shaker at 4°C.
Pour a small amount of OCT media on the sample disk and allow it to solidify.
Carefully place the disk in the holder and trim the OCT compound until it becomes a flat surface.
Ensure that the surface of the OCT is completely flat.
Mark the position where you intend to place the brain slice on the specimen disk.
Pick up the brain slice by a spatula and place it horizontally on the marked position.
Cover the surface of the brain slice with ample amount of OCT media.
Trim until the slices are reached, ensuring uniform cutting of the brain sections.
Set the desired thickness (30 μm) and start collecting the sections.
Start trimming of extra parts of OCT before reaching the brain slice.
Cut thin straight 30 μm sections.
Lay slices flat on the OCT media.
Press surface flat using a brush/spatula if necessary.
Carefully cut 3–4 sections at once.
Transfer sections into a 6-well plate filled with 1× PBS.
Allow sections to unroll in the 1× PBS solution.
Alternatively, make brain section flat using an anti-roll plate for slide mounting.
Directly mount the flattened brain section on a slide if desired.
Store slides in -80°C for long-term storage.
Collect enough 30 μm sections from both control and treatment groups.
Pre-select intact hippocampus sections using a brush and place them in a 6-well plate.
Wash the sections three times with 1× PBS.
Add 1 mL/well of blocking solution and block for 2 h at room temperature on a 3D shaker.
Remove the blocking solution.
Incubate with primary antibody (800 μL/well) for 2 days at 4°C.
Remove the primary antibody and store it in a separate tube marked as recycled.
Wash the sections three times with 1× PBS for 10 min each.
Prepare the secondary antibodies.
Incubate the sections with respective secondary antibodies anti-mouse 647 (1:500) and anti-rabbit 488 (1:500) for 2 h at room temperature.
Cover the plate with a shielded cover to keep it dark.
Wash sections three times with 1× PBS solution for 10 min each.
Transfer 3–4 sections from the 6-well plate into a petri dish filled with 1× PBS.
Carefully mount sections flat on the slide using a brush.
Keep the slide tilted with half of its surface inside PBS.
Move up the section where the slide touches PBS and slowly pull out the slide.
Use a soft fine-ended brush to adjust any small folds on the section to make it flat.
Keep the slides tilted on filter paper in the dark to dry.
Mount the sections with NucBlueTM mounting media.
Apply 10 μL of mounting media per hippocampus section to avoid pressure on the section.
Place a thin pipette head between the coverslip and slide to evenly distribute the mounting media.
Slowly remove the pipette to allow even distribution of the mounting media above the sample.
Remove any air bubbles by applying pressure from the sides, away from the brain specimen.
Store slides at -20°C for long-term preservation of fluorescent signals.
Before imaging on a confocal microscope, keep slides at RT (21°C to 24°C) for 20-30 minutes.
Reimage high-resolution individual astrocytes from the stratum radiatum layer of CA1 region in the hippocampus.
Stain slides double-immunofluorescently for astrocytes and either C1q protein or PSD95 as a postsynaptic marker.
Deconvolve images using the lightning function in Leica software to enhance resolution and contrast.
Label the nucleus/DNA with NucBlueTM present in the mounting media.
Identify distinct layers and regions of the hippocampus, particularly focusing on the CA1 area.
Perform imaging with three active fluorescent channels.
Select 2-hybrid detectors (HyD) for reduced noise when using the Leica SP8 microscope.
Utilize photomultiplier tube (PMT) sensors as needed.
Detect the nuclear (NucBlueTM) signal with the PMT sensor.
Detect GFAP and C1q/PSD95 signals using HyD sensors.
Switch on the confocal 30 minutes prior to imaging.
Calibrate the stage before imaging.
Stabilize the laser power before imaging.
Wait at least 15–20 minutes after switching on the confocal before starting the laser.
Locate the CA1 area of the hippocampus.
Start from a lower magnification (10×/0.40 NA) and then switch to higher magnification (20×/0.75 NA).
Use nuclear staining to help identify the region of interest (CA1).
Locate the dentate gyrus in the hippocampus first.
Track down the CA1 area of the hippocampus.
Find the stratum radiatum layer, which is directly below the densely stained pyramidal layer.
Switch to 63× (oil)/1.40 NA for single cell acquisition of astrocytes.
Put one drop of immersion oil.
Adjust all three channels: Blue, Green and Red with suggested parameters.
Slowly move across the XY plane to look for well-processed and structured astrocytes.
Set z-stack according to the GFAP channel to cover the entire volume of the astrocyte.
Click on “Start Experiment” to start taking acquisition of all the three channels.
Perform deconvolution of images before exporting them to Imaris for further analysis.
Switch off the smoothing function for the GFAP channel.
Adjust the regularization parameter to balance signal-to-noise ratio.
Use default settings of the LASX regularization parameter for image deconvolution.
Set the regularization value based on the SNR ratio, lower for good SNR.
Open the file in Imaris software.
Select “Add new surface” from the tab menu.
Segment only a region of interest under the “Algorithm Settings” box.
Unselect the smooth option for the astrocyte.
Adjust the filter settings for volumetric rendering of astrocyte.
Manually adjust the threshold to remove small particles in the volume filter.
Set the volume filter to 0.2 μm³ to exclude unwanted particles.
Click the green arrow button on step 4 to complete the rendering of the astrocyte.
If desired rendering is not achieved, start again from step 39 until the desired rendering is achieved.
Select all parameters for morphometric analysis in the "Export Statistics on Tab Display to file" dropdown list.
Choose "Export all statistics to file" if studying all parameters.
Export the file in either "xxx.csv" or "xxx.xls" format.
Filter out unwanted signals or processes from other astrocytes before proceeding.
Filter out unwanted signals and processes from the astrocyte image.
Select unwanted background signals using the “Circle Selection Mode”.
Choose the delete option under the “Edit” tab to remove selected signals.
Mask the surface of the astrocyte by clicking on the “Edit” tab.
Click the “Mask All” option to complete the masking process.
Select the GFAP (Red) channel in the mask channel box.
Set voxels outside the surface to 0 to eliminate background signal.
Open the Coloc tab in Imaris for colocalization analysis.
Analyze the contact between C1q protein (Green) and astrocyte surface using the masked red channel.
Set the threshold intensity for channel A by selecting unambiguous puncta.
Right click on each punctum and drag to create a boundary around it, ensuring the yellow boundary covers the entire green signal.
Average the intensities of 10 unambiguous green puncta selected in step 2 to determine the threshold for channel A.
Set the threshold intensity for channel B (masked red) at 1.
Select 10 unambiguous green dots randomly.
Average the intensity values of the selected green dots.
Set the manual threshold for the green channel based on the average intensity value.
Left click and drag to encircle a C1q protein signal completely.
Ensure the yellow boundary set by Imaris covers the entire signal.
Calculate the mean intensity value from multiple puncta to establish a balanced threshold.
Avoid using the 2D histogram for setting thresholds between channels as it may produce inconsistent results.
Carefully encircle positive C1q signals to prevent false results in colocalization analysis.
Set the intensity threshold for channel B in the masked GFAP image to 1.
Select the "Region of Interest" tab.
Choose the masked GFAP channel and set its threshold to 1.
Build a coloc channel in the analysis software.
Export the dataset as a "xxx.csv" file.
Define the region of interest (ROI) as the astrocyte mask.
Calculate the percentage of ROI colocalized to estimate the amount of C1q tag present in the whole volume of the astrocyte.
